claim: Intestinal epithelium-derived BMP serves as a niche signal for intestinal stem cell (ISC) self-renewal in Drosophila adult midgut.
source: Here we demonstrate that intestinal epithelium-derived BMP serves as a niche signal for intestinal stem cell (ISC) self-renewal in Drosophila adult midgut.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including RNAi, clonal analysis, and lineage tracing.

claim: BMP signaling is asymmetric between ISC and its differentiated daughter cell.
source: We find that BMP signaling is asymmetric between ISC and its differentiated daughter cell.
evidence: Supported by pMad immunostaining showing differential BMP pathway activity between ISCs and EBs.

claim: Two BMP ligands, Dpp and Gbb, are produced by enterocytes.
source: Two BMP ligands, Dpp and Gbb, are produced by enterocytes and act in conjunction to promote ISC self-renewal by antagonizing Notch signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated by dpp-Gal4 expression pattern and RNA in situ hybridization showing dpp and gbb mRNA in enterocytes.

claim: Dpp and Gbb act in conjunction to promote ISC self-renewal by antagonizing Notch signaling.
source: Two BMP ligands, Dpp and Gbb, are produced by enterocytes and act in conjunction to promote ISC self-renewal by antagonizing Notch signaling.
evidence: Supported by genetic epistasis experiments showing that Notch activation suppresses BMP-induced ISC phenotypes and that loss of Notch rescues BMP loss-of-function phenotypes.

claim: The basement membrane-associated type IV collagens regulate ISC self-renewal by confining higher BMP signaling to ISCs.
source: Furthermore, the basement membrane-associated type IV collagens regulate ISC self-renewal by confining higher BMP signaling to ISCs.
evidence: Demonstrated by vkg mutant analysis showing increased ISC numbers and altered BMP distribution.

claim: Inactivation of BMP signaling in adult midgut precursor cells by knocking down either type I or type II receptor blocked DSS- or bleomycin-induced ISC proliferation.
source: We found that inactivation of BMP signaling in adult midgut precursor cells by knocking down either type I (esgts>Tkv-RNAi; VDRC#105834) or type II (esgts>Put-RNAi; VDRC #107071) receptor blocked DSS- or bleomycin-induced ISC proliferation, as indicated by the diminished mitotic cells recognized by staining with an anti-phospho-histone 3 (PH3) antibody (Figure 1B).
evidence: Quantification shown in Figure 1B demonstrates significant reduction in PH3+ cells.

claim: Damage-induced ISC proliferation and epithelial turnover were blocked by inactivation of either type I or type II BMP receptor.
source: Damage-induced ISC proliferation and epithelial turnover were blocked by inactivation of either type I or type II BMP receptor because GFP+ ECs or EEs, or PH3+ cells were rarely found in midguts expressing UAS-Tkv-RNAi105834 or UAS-Put-RNAi with esgF/O (Figure 1F–K,O–T).
evidence: Figure 1F-K and O-T show absence of differentiated cells and mitotic cells in BMP receptor knockdown guts.

claim: The number of Dl+ cells dropped significantly in Tkv or Put RNAi guts 8 days after adult flies were cultured at 29°C.
source: 8 days after adult flies were cultured at 29°C, the number of Dl+ cells dropped significantly in Tkv or Put RNAi guts: less than 10% of esg>GFP+ precursor cells were DI+ compared with ∼50% in control guts, whereas the number of Su(H)-lacZ+ cells increased concomitantly (Figure 2A–G).
evidence: Quantification in Figure 2G shows dramatic shift from Dl+ to Su(H)-lacZ+ cells.

claim: Most pairs of precursor cells deficient for BMP signaling contained two Su(H)-lacZ+ and no Dl+ cells.
source: By contrast, most pairs of precursor cells deficient for BMP signaling contained two Su(H)-lacZ+ and no Dl+ cells (Figure 2B–C,E–F″).
evidence: Figure 2B-C and E-F″ show pairs of Su(H)-lacZ+ cells without Dl staining.

claim: The stem cell loss phenotype caused by inactivation of BMP signaling cannot be rescued by blocking apoptosis.
source: The stem cell loss phenotype caused by inaction of BMP signaling cannot be rescued by blocking apoptosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that BMP signaling does not simply regulate ISC survival.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows that Diap1 overexpression does not rescue Dl+ cell loss in Put RNAi guts.

claim: Loss of BMP signaling alters the outcome of ISC divisions from mostly asymmetric to predominantly symmetric non-self renewing.
source: Thus, loss of BMP signaling alters the outcome of ISC divisions from mostly asymmetric to predominantly symmetric non-self renewing.
evidence: Twin-spot analysis shows 80% EB/EB class in Put RNAi compared to 82% ISC/EB class in control.

claim: putP behaves like a genetic null allele.
source: putP (also known as put10460) behaves like a genetic null allele (Ruberte et al., 1995).
evidence: Cited from Ruberte et al., 1995.

claim: The majority of putP ISC lineage clones contained two cells of small nuclei with no Dl staining but both exhibiting Su(H)-lacZ expression at 12 days after clone induction.
source: By contrast, the majority of putP ISC lineage clones contained two cells of small nuclei with no Dl staining but both exhibiting Su(H)-lacZ expression (Figure 3B,I,J).
evidence: Figure 3B, I, J show quantification and images of putP clones with two Su(H)-lacZ+ cells.

claim: At 5 days after clone induction, 91% of control clones contained one Dl+ cell and one Su(H)-lacZ+ cell whereas 82% of putP clones contained two Su(H)-lacZ+ cells.
source: Even at an early time point (5 days ACI) whereby most of the ISC lineage clones contain only two cells, 91% (109/120) of the control clones contained one Dl+ cell and one Su(H)-lacZ+ cell whereas 82% (98/120) of the putP clones contained two Su(H)-lacZ+ cells (Figure 3G,H), suggesting that BMP-signaling-deficient ISC daughters failed to self-renew but instead underwent precocious differentiation into two EBs.
evidence: Figure 3G-H show early time point analysis of clone composition.

claim: At 12 days after clone induction, the majority of control clones contained Pdm1+ ECs whereas none of the putP clones exhibited Pdm1 staining.
source: Of note, at 12 days ACI, the majority of control clones contained Pdm1+ ECs whereas none of the putP clones (0/150) exhibited Pdm1 staining (Figure 3C,D,K); however, at 18 days ACI, a large fraction of putP clones (∼70%, n = 95) exhibited Pdm1 staining (Figure 3E,F,K).
evidence: Figure 3C-F and K show temporal progression of Pdm1 expression in putP clones.

claim: The delayed occurrence of Pdm1+ cells in putP clones suggests that BMP signaling is also required for proper ISC lineage differentiation into mature cells.
source: The delayed occurrence of Pdm1+ cells in putP clones further argues that BMP signaling is also required for proper ISC lineage differentiation into mature cells.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal delay in Pdm1 expression in putP clones.

claim: tkv8 is a null allele that encodes a truncated protein containing only part of the extracellular domain.
source: tkv8 is a null allele that encodes a truncated protein containing only part of the extracellular domain (Nellen et al., 1994).
evidence: Cited from Nellen et al., 1994.

claim: tkv8 clones exhibited increased clone size and contained one or more Dl+ cells.
source: Surprisingly, compared to the control clones, tkv8 clones exhibited increased clone size and contained one or more Dl+ cells (Figure 3L,M,T,U) suggesting that tkv8 clones over-proliferated.
evidence: Figure 3L-M and T-U show quantification and images of tkv8 clone phenotypes.

claim: BMP can transduce signal through two type I receptors Tkv and Sax.
source: BMP can transduce signal through two type I receptors Tkv and Sax (Brummel et al., 1994; Nellen et al., 1994), raising a possibility that Sax may support ISC self-renewal in the absence of Tkv.
evidence: Cited from Brummel et al., 1994 and Nellen et al., 1994.

claim: tkv8 clones expressing Sax-RNAi behaved similarly to putP clones.
source: Indeed, we found that tkv8 clones expressing Sax-RNAi behaved similarly to putP clones even though Sax-RNAi alone did not exhibit a stem cell loss phenotype (Figure 3N,O,T).
evidence: Figure 3N-O and T show that combined loss of Tkv and Sax results in stem cell loss.

claim: The sequence targeted by Tkv-RNAi105834 contained a region that is conserved between Tkv and Sax.
source: We noticed that the sequence targeted by Tkv-RNAi105834 contained a region that is conserved between Tkv and Sax (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Tkv-RNAi105834 could inactivate both Tkv and Sax, which may explain why Tkv-RNAi105834 caused ISC loss while tkv8 did not.
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1A shows schematic of RNAi target regions.

claim: Tkv-RNAi40937, which targets a unique region in Tkv, did not cause ISC loss but when combined with Sax-RNAi, resulted in stem cell loss.
source: Indeed, Tkv-RNAi40937, which targets a unique region in Tkv did not cause ISC loss but when combined with Sax-RNAi, resulted in stem cell loss (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–E′).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-E′ show that specific Tkv knockdown requires additional Sax knockdown for stem cell loss.

claim: Different degrees of BMP pathway inactivation may result in distinct phenotypes with partial loss of BMP pathway activity causing ISC overproliferation whereas more complete loss of BMP signaling leading to ISC loss.
source: These results underscore the functional redundancy between Tkv and Sax in the control of ISC self-renewal. Furthermore, they suggest that different degrees of BMP pathway inactivation may result in distinct phenotypes with partial loss of BMP pathway activity causing ISC overproliferation whereas more complete loss of BMP signaling leading to ISC loss.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of tkv8 single mutant (overproliferation) versus tkv8 Sax-RNAi or putP (stem cell loss).

claim: mad1–2 clones over-proliferated and behaved like tkv8 clones.
source: As expected, mad1–2 clones over-proliferated and behaved like tkv8 clones (Figure 3P,T,U); however, mad1–2 clones expressing Mad-RNAi exhibited stem cell loss phenotype (Figure 3R,T,U).
evidence: Figure 3P and R show mad1-2 clone phenotypes with and without additional Mad RNAi.

claim: tkv8 mad1–2 double mutant clones failed to proliferate and exhibited stem cell loss phenotype similar to put null mutant clones in the posterior midguts.
source: Strikingly, even though tkv8 or mad1–2 single mutant clones overproliferated, tkv8 mad1–2 double mutant clones failed to proliferate (Figure 3U, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D) and exhibited stem cell loss phenotype similar to put null mutant clones in the posterior midguts (Figure 3S,T).
evidence: Figure 3S-U and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D show tkv8 mad1-2 double mutant phenotype.

claim: PH3 staining of midguts containing either mad1–2 or tkv8 clones revealed increased mitotic index both outside and inside the mutant clones.
source: Interestingly, PH3 staining of midguts containing either mad1–2 or tkv8 clones revealed increased mitotic index both outside and inside the mutant clones (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C), suggesting that mad1–2 and tkv8 clones can exert a non-cell-autonomous effect on the proliferation of neighboring wild type ISCs.
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C show PH3 staining in and around mutant clones.

claim: tkv8 mad1–2 double mutant clones did not exhibit any PH3+ signal, nor did they stimulate the proliferation of neighboring wild type ISCs.
source: In contrast, tkv8 mad1–2 double mutant clones did not exhibit any PH3+ signal, nor did they stimulate the proliferation of neighboring wild type ISCs because no ectopic PH3+ cells were associated with mad1–2 tkv8 double mutant clones in the posterior midguts (Figure 3U, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Figure 3U and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D show absence of PH3+ cells in and around double mutant clones.

claim: The non-cell-autonomous effect of tkv8 and mad1–2 single mutant clones was due to BMP signaling defects in ECs.
source: Because tkv8 and mad1–2 single mutant clones contained many ECs whereas put null or tkv8 mad1–2 double mutant clones contained little if any ECs at the time we did PH3 staining, we suspected that the non-cell-autonomous effect of tkv8 and mad1–2 single mutant clones was due to BMP signaling defects in ECs. In support of this notion, RNAi of Put, Tkv, or Mad in ECs resulted in elevated ISC proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Li et al., 2013b).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 3 shows increased PH3+ cells when BMP signaling is reduced in ECs.

claim: High levels of pMad signal were observed in Dl-lacZ+ cells and low levels in Su(H)>GFP+ cells.
source: By immunostaining with an anti-pMad antibody (Persson et al., 1998), we observed high levels of pMad signal in Dl-lacZ+ cells and low levels in Su(H)>GFP+ cells (Figure 4A–B′), suggesting that BMP pathway is asymmetrically activated in a pair of ISC/EB cells with ISC transducing higher levels of BMP signaling activity than EB.
evidence: Figure 4A-B′ show differential pMad staining in ISC versus EB.

claim: dad-lacZ exhibits high levels of expression in ISCs and low levels of expression in EBs.
source: Consistent with this notion, we found that dad-lacZ, which is induced by BMP signaling, exhibits high levels of expression in ISCs and low levels of expression in EBs (Figure 4C).
evidence: Figure 4C shows dad-lacZ expression pattern in ISC/EB pairs.

claim: pMad signals were evenly distributed into two future daughter cells of a dividing ISC marked by PH3+.
source: However, pMad signals were evenly distributed into two future daughter cells of a dividing ISC marked by PH3+(Figure 4D), suggesting that asymmetric BMP signaling is unlikely due to asymmetric inheritance of activated pathway components but rather due to asymmetric induction after ISC division.
evidence: Figure 4D shows equal pMad in dividing ISC.

claim: A small fraction (8/105) of ISC division resulted in the production of two Dl+ ISCs that contained equally high levels of pMad staining.
source: A small fraction (8/105) of ISC division resulted in the production of two Dl+ ISCs that contained equally high levels of pMad staining (Figure 4E,E′) and both ISCs tend to lie in close proximity to the BM (Figure 4F,F′), suggesting that they were derived from symmetric cell division (Goulas et al., 2012).
evidence: Figure 4E-F′ show symmetric ISC/ISC pairs with high pMad.

claim: Strong pMad staining and dad-lacZ expression were observed in ECs.
source: We also observed strong pMad staining and dad-lacZ expression in ECs (indicated by asterisks in Figure 4B–D, F,F′), suggesting that BMP signaling is active in differentiated cells.
evidence: Figure 4B-D and F-F′ show pMad and dad-lacZ in ECs.

claim: Expression of TkvQ235D for 4 days resulted in many pairs of Dl+ Su(H)-lacZ- precursor cells.
source: 4 days after shifting to 29°C, esgts>TkvQ235D guts contained many pairs of Dl+ Su(H)-lacZ- precursor cells (arrows in Figure 4H).
evidence: Figure 4H shows pairs of Dl+ cells without Su(H)-lacZ.

claim: Expression of TkvQ235D for 8 days resulted in the formation of large clusters of ISC-like cells that contained dividing cells.
source: Expression of TkvQ235D for a longer period of time (8 days) resulted in the formation of large clusters of ISC-like cells that contained diving cells (Figure 4K,N), suggesting that ectopic BMP signaling promotes ISC self-renewal.
evidence: Figure 4K and N show large Dl+ clusters with PH3+ cells.

claim: Midguts expressing esgts>TkvQ235D generated symmetric twin clones of the ISC/ISC class at much higher frequency (77%; 146/190) than the control guts (9%; 14/160).
source: As shown in Figure 4Q–S, midguts expressing esgts>TkvQ235D generated symmetric twin clones of the ISC/ISC class at much higher frequency (77%; 146/190) than the control guts (9%; 14/160), suggesting that ectopic BMP signaling activity promotes the symmetric self-renewing outcome of an ISC division.
evidence: Figure 4Q-S show quantification of twin-spot classes with TkvQ235D overexpression.

claim: Coexpression of Dpp and Gbb using esgts resulted in the formation of ISC-like cell clusters similar to ectopic expression of TkvQ235D.
source: Coexpression of Dpp and Gbb using esgts also resulted in the formation of ISC-like cell clusters similar to ectopic expression of TkvQ235D (Figure 4I,L,O); however, expression of either Dpp or Gbb alone only produced smaller ISC-like cell clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; compared with Figure 4L).
evidence: Figure 4I, L, O show Dpp+Gbb phenotype; Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows individual ligand effects.

claim: Dpp and Gbb act in concert to promote ISC self-renewal likely by forming a heterodimer.
source: These results suggest that Dpp and Gbb act in concert to promote ISC self-renewal likely by forming a heterodimer (see below) (Ray and Wharton, 2001).
evidence: Inferred from synergistic effects of Dpp and Gbb coexpression; cited from Ray and Wharton, 2001.

claim: N activation completely suppressed the formation of ISC-like cell clusters induced by ectopic BMP signaling.
source: We found that N activation completely suppressed the formation of ISC-like cell clusters induced by ectopic BMP signaling (Figure 5D–E′ compared with Figure 5B–C′).
evidence: Figure 5D-E′ show that NICD blocks TkvQ235D and Dpp+Gbb phenotypes.

claim: Loss of N signaling restored Dl+ cells in BMP signaling deficient precursor cells.
source: We found that loss of N signaling restored Dl+ cells in BMP signaling deficient precursor cells (Figure 5I–J′ compared with Figure 5G–H′), suggesting that ISC can form in the absence of BMP signaling as long as N signaling is blocked.
evidence: Figure 5I-J′ show rescue of Dl+ cells by N RNAi in BMP-deficient background.

claim: Most of the ISC-like cells in N RNAi guts exhibited low levels of BMP pathway activity.
source: Furthermore, pMad staining indicates that most of the ISC-like cells in N RNAi guts exhibited low levels of BMP pathway activity (Figure 5L–L′ compared with Figure 5K–K′; Figure 5—figure supplement 1), consistent with N acting downstream of or in parallel with BMP.
evidence: Figure 5L-L′ and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 show reduced pMad in N RNAi precursor clusters.

claim: BMP signaling promotes ISC self-renewal by antagonizing N-mediated differentiation.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that BMP signaling promotes ISC self-renewal by antagonizing N-mediated differentiation.
evidence: Concluded from epistasis experiments showing N acts downstream of BMP.

claim: Midguts expressing esgts>Tkv-RNAi105834 + N-RNAi or esgts>Put-RNAi + N-RNAi contained smaller clusters of Dl+ cells compared with esgts>N-RNAi guts.
source: We noticed that midguts expressing esgts>Tkv-RNAi105834 + N-RNAi or esgts>Put-RNAi + N-RNAi contained smaller clusters of Dl+ cells compared with esgts>N-RNAi guts (Figure 5F–F′, Figure 5I–J′), suggesting that BMP pathway activity is required for the proliferation of N-signaling-deficient ISCs.
evidence: Figure 5F-F′ and I-J′ show reduced cluster size with combined BMP and N loss.

claim: Expression of NICD in precursor cells resulted in diminished pMad staining.
source: We also noticed that expression of NICD in precursor cells resulted in diminished pMad staining (Figure 5M–M′ compared with Figure 5K–K′), suggesting that excessive N signaling can inhibit BMP pathway activity.
evidence: Figure 5M-M′ show reduced pMad with NICD expression.

claim: GFP under the control of dpp-Gal4 was detected in ECs along the anterior-posterior axis but not in precursor cells or VM.
source: To our surprise, GFP under the control of a dpp-Gal4 (dpp>GFP) (Teleman and Cohen, 2000; Roy et al., 2011) was detected in ECs along the anterior-posterior (A-P) axis (Figure 6A,B,D,D′) but not in precursor cells or VM (data not shown).
evidence: Figure 6A-B and D-D′ show dpp>GFP expression in ECs.

claim: dpp>GFP signals exhibited discrete domains of high-level expression in the posterior, middle and anterior regions.
source: However, dpp>GFP signals were not uniform along the A-P axis of the midguts but instead, exhibited discrete domains of high-level expression in the posterior (p), middle (m) and anterior (a) regions (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Figure 6A-B show regional variation in dpp>GFP intensity.

claim: RNA in situ hybridization confirmed that the expression pattern of dpp>GFP correlated with that of endogenous dpp mRNA.
source: In situ hybridization confirmed that the expression pattern of dpp>GFP correlated with that of endogenous dpp mRNA (Figure 6E,E′, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: Figure 6E-E′ and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-H show colocalization of dpp mRNA and dpp>GFP.

claim: dpp mRNA was not detected in precursor cells or VM.
source: Furthermore, dpp mRNA was not detected in precursor cells or VM (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–F′).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-F′ show absence of dpp mRNA in esg>GFP+ and how>GFP+ cells.

claim: gbb mRNA was detected in ECs but not in precursor cells or VM.
source: Similarly, gbb mRNA was detected in ECs but not in precursor cells or VM (Figure 6F–F′, Figure 6—figure supplement 2G–L′), and high levels of gbb were detected in regions that expressed low levels of dpp (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: Figure 6F-F′ and Figure 6—figure supplement 2G-L′ show gbb mRNA in ECs; Figure 6—figure supplement 1I-L show complementary dpp/gbb patterns.

claim: Increasing the production of Dpp and Gbb in ECs using the Myo1A-Gal4/tub-Gal80ts system resulted in increased number of Dl+ cells.
source: Increasing the production of Dpp and Gbb in ECs using the Myo1A-Gal4/tub-Gal80ts (Myo1Ats) system to express UAS-Dpp and UAS-Gbb resulted in increased number of Dl+ cells (Figure 7B), indicating that paracrine BMP signaling initiated from ECs can promote ISC self-renewal.
evidence: Figure 7B shows increased Dl+ cells with EC-specific Dpp+Gbb overexpression.

claim: Knockdown of Dpp or Gbb by strong RNAi lines resulted in loss of Dl+ cells.
source: Knockdown of Dpp or Gbb by strong RNAi lines (Myo1Ats>Dpp-RNAiS or Myo1Ats>Gbb-RNAiS) resulted in loss of Dl+ cells (Figure 7D,E,H–J; Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Figure 7D-E and H-J show loss of Dl+ cells with EC-specific Dpp or Gbb knockdown.

claim: pMad staining confirmed that BMP signaling activity was diminished both in precursor cells and ECs in Myo1Ats>Dpp-RNAiS or Myo1Ats>Gbb-RNAiS guts.
source: pMad staining confirmed that BMP signaling activity was diminished both in precursor cells and ECs in these guts (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–C′).
evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-C′ show reduced pMad with EC-specific Dpp or Gbb knockdown.

claim: Myo1Ats>Dpp-RNAiS or Myo1Ats>Gbb-RNAiS guts exhibited greatly reduced mitotic index in response to injury.
source: Consistent with the stem cell loss phenotype, Myo1Ats>Dpp-RNAiS or Myo1Ats>Gbb-RNAiS guts exhibited greatly reduced mitotic index in response to injury as compared with controlled guts (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D–J).
evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 2D-J show reduced PH3+ cells after DSS treatment in EC-specific Dpp or Gbb knockdown.

claim: Combined expression of weak Dpp and Gbb RNAi lines resulted in loss of Dl+ cells.
source: Although knockdown of Dpp or Gbb by weak RNAi lines (Myo1Ats>Dpp-RNAiW or Myo1Ats>Gbb-RNAiW) did not significantly affect Dl+ cell number (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G–I), their combined expression (Myo1Ats>Dpp-RNAiW + Gbb-RNAiW) resulted in loss of Dl+ cells (Figure 7F; Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1I show synergistic effect of weak Dpp and Gbb RNAi.

claim: Dpp is expressed in tracheal cells that contact adult midgut epithelium.
source: Recent studies suggested that Dpp is expressed in tracheal cells that contact adult midgut epithelium (Li et al., 2013b) or in VM (Guo et al., 2013). We confirmed that Dpp is expressed in tracheal cells by RNA in situ hybridization (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A)
evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 4A shows dpp mRNA in Btl>GFP+ tracheal cells; cited from Li et al., 2013b and Guo et al., 2013.

claim: Overexpression of either Dpp alone or in conjunction with Gbb in tracheal cells using Btl-Gal4 Gal80ts did not increase Dl+ cell number.
source: however, overexpression of either Dpp alone or in conjunction with Gbb in tracheal cells using Btl-Gal4 Gal80ts (Btlts) did not increase Dl+ cell number (Figure 7—figure supplement 4B–D).
evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 4B-D show no increase in Dl+ cells with tracheal Dpp or Dpp+Gbb overexpression.

claim: Neither Dpp RNAi in trachea nor in VM significantly affected Dl+ cell number.
source: Furthermore, neither Dpp RNAi in trachea (Btlts>Dpp-RNAiS) nor in VM (Howts>Dpp-RNAiS) significantly affected Dl+ cell number (Figure 7—figure supplement 4E–H), which is in contrast to Dpp or Gbb RNAi in ECs.
evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 4E-H show no significant change in Dl+ cells with tracheal or VM Dpp knockdown.

claim: EC-derived Dpp and Gbb are the major source of BMP that regulates ISC self-renewal.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that EC-derived Dpp and Gbb are the major source of BMP that regulates ISC self-renewal.
evidence: Concluded from tissue-specific knockdown and overexpression experiments.

claim: When expressed in ECs, a GFP-tagged Dpp was enriched on the basal side of midgut epithelia.
source: Interestingly, when expressed in ECs, a GFP-tagged Dpp (Dpp-GFP) was enriched on the basal side of midgut epithelia (Figure 8B,B′) whereas a control GFP was uniformly distributed along the apical basal axis (Figure 8A,A′).
evidence: Figure 8A-B′ show differential distribution of control GFP versus Dpp-GFP.

claim: Dpp-GFP was enriched on the basal side of the secretory pathway.
source: Co-staining with a Golgi marker revealed that Dpp-GFP was enriched on the basal side of the secretary pathway (Figure 8C), raising the possibility that Dpp-GFP is preferentially secreted from the basal/basolateral side of ECs.
evidence: Figure 8C shows Dpp-GFP localization relative to Golgi marker.

claim: A GFP-tagged Gbb was uniformly distributed along the apical/basal axis when expressed in ECs.
source: Although a GFP-tagged Gbb (Gbb-GFP) was uniformly distributed along the apical/basal axis when expressed in ECs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,A′), coexpression of Dpp redistributed Gbb-GFP toward the basal side (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–C′), suggesting that Dpp and Gbb may physically interact, a notion confirmed by coimmunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-C′ show Gbb-GFP redistribution with Dpp coexpression; Figure 8—figure supplement 2 shows co-IP of Dpp and Gbb.

claim: vkg trans-heterozygous midguts contained an excessive number of Dl+ cells and greatly reduced number of Su(H)-lacZ+ cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that vkg trans-heterozygous midguts (vkgk00236/vkg01209 and vkgk00236/vkg197) contained an excessive number of Dl+ cells and greatly reduced number of Su(H)-lacZ+ cells (Figure 8F–H), suggesting that compromised Vkg activity promotes ISC self-renewal.
evidence: Figure 8F-H show increased Dl+ and decreased Su(H)-lacZ+ cells in vkg mutants.

claim: vkg mutant guts contained clusters of precursor cells exhibiting high levels of BMP signaling activity.
source: pMad staining revealed that vkg mutant guts contained clusters of precursor cells exhibiting high levels of BMP signaling activity (compare Figure 8J with Figure 8I, Figure 8—figure supplement 3), suggesting that Vkg regulates ISC self-renewal through restricting BMP signaling.
evidence: Figure 8I-J and Figure 8—figure supplement 3 show elevated pMad in vkg mutant precursor clusters.

claim: Reducing the dose of Dpp suppressed ectopic ISC formation in vkg mutant guts.
source: As a further support, we found that reducing the dose of Dpp suppressed ectopic ISC formation in vkg mutant guts (Figure 8K–M).
evidence: Figure 8K-M show genetic interaction between vkg and dpp.

claim: vkg mutant guts retained less Dpp-GFP at the BM compared with control guts.
source: In addition, we found that vkg mutant guts retained less Dpp-GFP at the BM compared with control guts (Figure 8N–Q, Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Figure 8N-Q and Figure 8—figure supplement 4 show reduced Dpp-GFP at BM in vkg mutants.

claim: The BM in Drosophila midguts serves as an integral part of the ISC niche by regulating the extracellular distribution of the niche signal.
source: Hence, the BM in Drosophila midguts serves as an integral part of the ISC niche by regulating the extracellular distribution of the niche signal.
evidence: Concluded from vkg mutant analysis showing altered BMP distribution and ISC phenotypes.

claim: BMP signaling regulates copper cell differentiation in the middle region of midguts.
source: Several recent studies revealed that BMP signaling plays several roles in Drosophila adult midgut homeostasis (Guo et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013a, 2013b). First, peak levels of BMP signaling in the middle region of midguts specify copper cell differentiation (Guo et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013a).
evidence: Cited from Guo et al., 2013 and Li et al., 2013a.

claim: BMP signaling regulates ISC proliferation because reduction in BMP pathway activity results in ISC overproliferation.
source: Second, BMP signaling also regulates ISC proliferation because reduction in BMP pathway activity results in ISC overproliferation (Guo et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013b), which is in line with a growth inhibitory role of BMP signaling in mammalian intestines (Haramis et al., 2004; He et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from Guo et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013b; Haramis et al., 2004; He et al., 2004.

claim: Both tkv8 and mad1–2 mutant clones caused excessive proliferation of neighboring wild type ISCs.
source: The observations that both tkv8 and mad1–2 mutant clones caused excessive proliferation of neighboring wild type ISCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C) and that inactivation of BMP signaling in ECs stimulated ISC proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–E) clearly support a non-cell autonomous role of BMP signaling.
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B-E show non-cell autonomous effects.

claim: Inactivation of BMP signaling in ECs stimulated the production of JAK-STAT and EGFR pathway ligands that fuel ISC proliferation.
source: Indeed, inactivation of BMP signaling in ECs stimulated the production of JAK-STAT and EGFR pathway ligands that fuel ISC proliferation (Li et al., 2013b) (our own unpublished observation).
evidence: Cited from Li et al., 2013b and authors' unpublished data.

claim: Asymmetric BMP signaling plays an instructive role in the regulation of ISC self-renewal.
source: To determine whether asymmetric BMP signaling plays an instructive role in the regulation of ISC self-renewal, we ectopically activated the pathway in precursor cells by expressing a constitutively active form of Tkv (TkvQ235D) (Nellen et al., 1996).
evidence: Tested by gain-of-function experiments with TkvQ235D.

claim: The employment of midgut epithelia as stem cell niche may provide a mechanism for direct communication between the niche and the environment.
source: We speculate that the employment of midgut epithelia as stem cell niche may provide a mechanism for direct communication between the niche and the environment, allowing the production of niche signal and stem cell number to be regulated in response to various physiological and pathological stimuli.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the biological significance of EC-derived niche signals.

claim: Low levels of BMP pathway activity conferred by Sax-Put receptor complex appear to be enough to support ISC self-renewal.
source: This result suggests that low levels of BMP pathway activity conferred by Sax-Put receptor complex appear to be enough to support ISC self-renewal (although not enough to prevent ISC from overproliferation).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that tkv8 single mutants retain ISCs.

claim: Removal of either Dpp or Gbb resulted in ISC loss, implying that Dpp or Gbb homodimers failed to produce enough BMP activity to support ISC self-renewal.
source: On the other hand, our results showed that removal of either Dpp or Gbb resulted in ISC loss, implying that Dpp or Gbb homodimers failed to produce enough BMP activity to support ISC self-renewal.
evidence: Inferred from EC-specific Dpp or Gbb RNAi phenotypes.

claim: Basal secretion coupled with BM trapping may establish a steep BMP activity gradient.
source: Because type IV collagen/Vkg can physically interact with Dpp (Wang et al., 2008), we propose that basal secretion coupled with BM trapping may establish a steep BMP activity gradient so that basally localized ISC daughter cells receive higher levels of BMP than their more apically localized siblings, resulting in differential BMP signaling (Figure 9).
evidence: Model proposed based on Dpp-GFP localization and vkg mutant phenotypes; cited from Wang et al., 2008.

claim: BMP promotes ISC fate by inhibiting N pathway activity.
source: Although it is possible that BMP and N pathways could act in parallel and exert opposing influence on ISC/EB fate choice, we favor a model in which BMP promotes ISC fate by inhibiting N pathway activity because loss of BMP signaling in precursor cells resulted in the ectopic expression of Su(H)-lacZ, which is a N pathway activity reporter, whereas gain of BMP signaling suppressed the expression of Su(H)-lacZ in precursor cells (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis and marker expression analysis.

claim: Differential BMP signaling sets up a difference in the levels of N signaling activity between the two daughter cells after an ISC division.
source: Therefore, we propose that differential BMP signaling sets up a difference in the levels of N signaling activity between the two daughter cells after an ISC division.
evidence: Model proposed based on asymmetric BMP signaling and epistasis with Notch.

claim: The initial small difference in N pathway activity between apical and basal ISC daughter cells is amplified by N feedback regulation.
source: The initial small difference in the N pathway activity between the apical and basal ISC daughter cells is amplified by N feedback regulation (Figure 9; Axelrod, 2010): N signaling in the apical cell inhibits Dl expression and Dl accumulation in the basal cell further strengthens N signaling in its apical sibling.
evidence: Model incorporating known Notch-Delta feedback; cited from Axelrod, 2010.

claim: Elevated N pathway activity in the apical ISC daughter cell may attenuate BMP signaling in this cell, forming another feedback mechanism to reinforce EB fate choice.
source: Intriguingly, we also found that excessive N signaling could block BMP pathway activity, as indicated by the blockage of pMad staining in precursor cells expressing NICD (Figure 5M). We speculate that elevated N pathway activity in the apical ISC daughter cell may attenuate BMP signaling in this cell, forming another feedback mechanism to reinforce EB fate choice.
evidence: Speculative model based on observation that NICD reduces pMad.

claim: Asymmetric segregation of aPKC may dampen BMP signaling response in the apically localized ISC daughter cells.
source: A recent study revealed that aPKC is asymmetrically inherited by apically localized ISC daughter cells and that aPKC promotes N pathway activity (Goulas et al., 2012). Therefore, asymmetric segregation of aPKC may dampen BMP signaling response in the apically localized ISC daughter cells, which could contribute to the differential BMP signaling.
evidence: Speculative integration of aPKC asymmetry with BMP signaling; cited from Goulas et al., 2012.
